extracted.intended_audience: NLP researchers, dataset creators, annotators and practitioners working on clickbait detection (particularly for Spanish-language news / social media)
extracted.subtask_description: Define clickbait precisely and produce an annotated Spanish-language clickbait corpus (TA1C), with operational labeling criteria, dataset collection rules, annotation methodology, and baseline preprocessing/modeling decisions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Clickbait definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Clickbait is a technique for generating headlines and teasers that deliberately omit part of the information with the goal of raising the readers’ curiosity, capturing their attention and enticing them to click.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This is the proposed formal definition used to distinguish clickbait from other attention-grabbing strategies such as sensationalism. It centers the concept on the deliberate creation of an information/curiosity gap.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational annotation definition
rubrics_metrics.description: Teasers that omit part of the information not obvious by context, arising curiosity and enticing users to click.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Because author intent cannot be inferred, annotation must use this operationalization: if a teaser omits non-obvious information that creates curiosity and entices a click, label it as clickbait. Still allows for hard subjective cases, so refined criteria follow.

rubrics_metrics.name: Take all context of the news publication into account
rubrics_metrics.description: Assume anything within the common knowledge of an average reader of that publication is known; consider factors such as where, to whom, and when the news was released.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Annotators should account for publication date, geography and target audience; when reading teasers from foreign media, assume the target audience knows local context. Annotators may seek additional information when necessary. (Examples: Kabul airport massacre shortly after the event → not clickbait; Cuomo resignation widely known → not clickbait; first COVID case early in pandemic → not clickbait).

rubrics_metrics.name: Distinguish clickbait from sensationalism
rubrics_metrics.description: Sensational language or 'yellow' content is not necessarily clickbait; clickbait specifically involves creating an information gap rather than merely sensational wording or deceptive content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If the teaser does not omit crucial information or the curiosity is generated by the news content itself (not the presentation), label as non-clickbait. Example: a headline that reports dramatic events exactly as in the article is non-clickbait even if sensational.

rubrics_metrics.name: Intense adjectivation may lead to clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: Excessive use of adjectives or highlighted qualifications can create an information gap by emphasizing aspects without necessary context, thus producing curiosity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Judge whether adjectives create a gap (e.g., 'the spectacular phenomenon' without explaining why) versus being contextually understood (e.g., 'bloody' in drug-war reporting). If adjectivation omits essential explanatory information, label clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Self-responded gaps are not clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: If the publisher tweets variants of the same article where a later tweet (or teaser) answers the uncertainty created in a prior teaser, the gap is closed and should be labeled non-clickbait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Detect cases where the information gap is resolved in the surrounding social-context (e.g., another tweet providing the answer) — that eliminates the need to click.

rubrics_metrics.name: Not all questions are clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: The presence of a question mark or a question-form teaser does not automatically imply clickbait.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Questions should be labeled clickbait only if they create an information gap that is not answered in the teaser, not obviously unanswerable, not a cited question, and not merely rhetorical/reader-addressed without promising new info. If the teaser already answers the question or context makes the answer obvious, label non-clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Direct addresses to the reader only sometimes imply clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: Addressing the reader can be a clickbait technique when it creates an information gap, but direct address alone is insufficient for a clickbait label.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Determine whether the 'you' address promises missing information or merely engages the reader without withholding information. Example: 'Will you need to switch to a new phone?' → clickbait if it withholds the substantive answer; generic appeals or calls that don't promise specifics → non-clickbait.

rubrics_metrics.name: Editorials and opinion pieces can be clickbait
rubrics_metrics.description: Opinion or editorial pieces are not categorically excluded; they can be clickbait if the teaser deliberately omits information and creates a curiosity gap.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not automatically exclude editorials from consideration; apply the same information-gap criteria as for news headlines.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dataset media selection criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Prioritize reputable, national or international (not local), general (not topic-focused) and popular media; sample newspapers from as many Spanish-speaking countries as possible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA1C selected 18 well-known media outlets across 12 Spanish-speaking countries to represent language diversity and mainstream news; selection was guided by reputation, reach (Twitter followers / Comscore), and balance across countries.

rubrics_metrics.name: Data inclusion and exclusion rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Discard retweets, tweets without links, links to domains other than the media's main site, and cases where news content crawling failed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Only include tweets that link to the primary media site and whose articles could be successfully crawled; this avoids noisy or off-site content and ensures access to headline/article context.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sampling and split strategy
rubrics_metrics.description: Random sampling of tweets with per-source guarantees and balanced train/validation/test splits.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA1C sampled 3,500 tweets, guaranteeing at least 150 per media source; split into train=2100, validation=700, test=700 with random splits that preserve media and label balance.

rubrics_metrics.name: Annotation methodology and agreement target
rubrics_metrics.description: Label each instance with multiple independent annotators, deliberate on disagreements, refine criteria to reduce subjectivity, and use majority vote for final label while publishing all annotations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: TA1C used three annotators (two authors + one communication-sciences expert), iteratively discussed initial disagreements, and aimed for high inter-annotator reliability (TA1C achieved Fleiss’ κ = 0.825). Publish raw annotations and final majority labels.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid dataset-construction confounds (criticize reputation/gatekeeper methods)
rubrics_metrics.description: Reputation-based and gatekeeper-based dataset construction can introduce confounds where classes differ in source, style, and topic rather than in the phenomenon of interest.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prefer approaches that sample from the same set of sources and rely on clear operational definitions (importance method with refined annotation criteria) to minimize spurious signals unrelated to clickbait (e.g., media-specific style).

rubrics_metrics.name: Preprocessing and input construction for baselines
rubrics_metrics.description: Standardize text by substituting emojis/hashtags/account mentions for special tokens, remove URLs/special characters/multiple spaces, and combine headline and tweet according to overlap rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For reported baselines the authors: replaced emojis/hashtags/@-mentions with tokens, removed URLs and special chars, and combined headline with tweet text — keeping the longer when one contains the other or concatenating headline followed by tweet otherwise. For baselines they did not use article body, images, or tweet metadata (though dataset includes them).
